endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: The opportunity for a patient or their caregiver to request additional review from a licensed clinician should be made available upon request.

endorsements.title: When Is It Safe to Introduce an AI System Into Healthcare? A Practical Decision Algorithm for the Ethical Implementation of Black-Box AI in Medicine
endorsements.quote: Therefore, Consent‐GPT should be offered as an option (either in addition to, or instead of, typical consent conversations), and patients can choose to validly consent or refuse and interact with a human clinician instead .

endorsements.title: Augmenting research consent: should large language models (LLMs) be used for informed consent to clinical research?
endorsements.quote: Initial introduction of LLM-based consent processes should also allow participants to have the option to follow up with a researcher after an LLM interaction if they so choose.

endorsements.title: Ethical Governance of Large Language Models in Health Care: Trust, Responsibility, and Equity in Routine Use
endorsements.quote: Such mechanisms should be clearly assigned to responsible actors (eg, clinical teams and institutional oversight committees) and embedded in patient-facing communication channels to ensure that users can request clarification, correction, or human review in a timely manner.

endorsements.title: A Futures Framework for Clinical AI Governance: Anticipating Emerging Risks, Shifting Roles, and Regulatory Challenges
endorsements.quote: Governance priorities, therefore, include defined escalation thresholds, plain-language disclosure of AI use, access to human review on request, and exclusion criteria for patient groups requiring additional safeguards [ 16 ].

endorsements.title: Reclaiming the Human Connection in Clinical Care With AI
endorsements.quote: Importantly, all patient-facing AI navigation tools should be designed with the same consent and privacy standards applied to ambient documentation: patients should understand what the AI can and cannot do, how their data is used, and how to reach a human clinician when needed.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence in Family Nursing: An Evidence-Informed Policy Framework for Safe and Equitable Integration
endorsements.quote: Families should be told when artificial intelligence–supported tools are being used, what the tools can and cannot do, and how to contact a nurse when they need human support.

evidence.title: AI-Human Hybrid Workflow Enhances Teleophthalmology for the Detection of Diabetic Retinopathy
evidence.outcome: Interpretability of AI-ungradable screening encounters after human fallback
evidence.effect: A single specialist interpreted 88.1% of AI-ungradable encounters; adjudicated consensus found 77.7% interpretable. AI alone returned ungradable results in 36.5% of encounters.
evidence.quote: A single experienced retina specialist was able to interpret 93.1% of all patient encounters as well as 88.1% of AI-ungradable encounters, and an adjudicated consensus agreed that the image was interpretable in 77.7% of cases.

evidence.title: Factors for Patient Trust and Acceptance of Medical Artificial Intelligence
evidence.effect: Clinician presence increased probability of choosing the AI visit by 18.4% (95% CI, 17.3%-19.5%) vs no clinician.
evidence.quote: The AMCE was 0.184 (95% CI, 0.173-0.195), meaning that respondents were 18.4% (95% CI, 17.3%-19.5%) more likely to choose a visit with a clinician than one with no clinician (baseline).

commentary.bottom_line: Two studies support parts of this practice: in a real deployment, a specialist interpreted 88.1% of encounters the AI could not grade, and in a vignette survey, clinician presence raised the probability of choosing an AI visit by 18.4%. No study tested review requested by a patient or caregiver, so the evidence for the recommendation as written is indirect.

perspectives.view: Neither study tests the recommendation as worded. The screening study sent AI-ungradable encounters to a human reader automatically rather than at patient request. The survey measured stated choices in hypothetical vignettes. Both designs start at low certainty, and indirectness lowers certainty to very low.

AI returned ungradable results in 36.5% of 1,222 screening encounters, and a specialist interpreted 88.1% of those. This suggests a human fallback can resolve results that AI alone leaves open. The study did not report whether human review caught AI outputs that were wrong, which is the hazard this recommendation targets.

The screening study built fallback into a live workflow. Adjudicated consensus found 77.7% of AI-ungradable encounters interpretable, lower than the 88.1% reported by a single reader, and this gap may reflect variation between readers. No study described how patients would request review through portals, phone lines, or other channels.

The AI could not grade about one in three encounters in the screening deployment. At that rate, a health system would need specialist reading capacity for a large share of volume. The study did not report reader time or cost. No study estimated how many review requests patients would make.

Among 3,000 survey respondents, clinician presence raised the probability of choosing an AI visit by 18.4% (95% CI, 17.3%-19.5%). This suggests patients may value human involvement when AI is part of their care. The result reflects hypothetical choices, and no study asked patients whether they could actually reach a clinician when they wanted one.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared offering patient- or caregiver-requested clinician review with not offering it. Such a study would need to measure how often patients use the option, time to human contact, AI errors detected and corrected, patient trust, and staffing cost in real deployments across several care settings.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither study reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and both were conducted in the United States. Patients facing language or literacy barriers may have more difficulty finding and using a request channel. The current evidence cannot show whether human fallback works for these groups.
